summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2 / US Grade 2), teach odd and even as a structural property of number: even means a count can be split fully into pairs (or two equal groups) with none left over (= 2×something); odd leaves exactly one unpaired. Build the meaning by pairing physical or on-screen counters, connect it to the 2s table and the ones-digit pattern (ends in 0,2,4,6,8), and make clear that 0 is even and that odd/even has nothing to do with a number's size.
misconceptions: Thinking odd/even is about a number's SIZE rather than divisibility by 2.
Judging by the first (leading) digit instead of the ones digit.
Believing a number could be both odd and even, or neither.
Not connecting even numbers to the 2s table / '2×n' — treating the ending rule as unrelated to multiplication.

activities.title: Pairing machine: pair the counters and spot the leftover
steps: Choose a quantity of counters (start with numbers to 10, then extend to 20).
Pair the counters up into twos — physically with real counters, or by tapping a 'pair up' control if using a screen model.
Optionally lay the counters on a ten-frame to see full pairs versus one lonely counter.
Decide: if every counter has a partner, the number is EVEN; if exactly one counter is left on its own, the number is ODD.
Test number after number and watch the result build on a hundred square (even numbers shaded) so the alternating-column / ends-in-0,2,4,6,8 pattern appears.
Use a '2×n' / two-equal-rows view to see each even number as two equal groups, linking it to the 2s table.
Test 0: zero counters, zero left over — so 0 is even.
activities.insight: Even means everything pairs up with none left over (two equal groups / 2×n); odd means exactly one is left unpaired. The ones-digit rule and the 2s table both come from this pairing structure, not from an arbitrary ending.

activities.title: Introduce with a paired vs leftover picture
steps: Look at a picture that contrasts a set whose objects all pair up (even) with a set that has one object left over (odd).
Tap or point to an even set to reveal its neat pairs; tap an odd set to reveal the single leftover.
Look at a hundred square with even numbers shaded to see the alternating pattern.
activities.insight: A set that pairs up completely is even; a set with one left over is odd — and even numbers fall in a regular pattern.

activities.title: Sort numbers and check the edge cases
steps: Sort a mix of numbers (including 0 and two-digit numbers to 20) into 'odd' and 'even' boxes.
Answer: is 0 odd or even? Explain why.
Find the number that breaks a stated rule, and resist a distractor that judges by the leading (first) digit instead of the ones digit.
activities.insight: The classification holds for every whole number, including0. In base ten, each ten can be paired fully, so the ones digit determines whether a counter remains unpaired; a number’s size or leading digit does not decide its parity.

activities.title: Predict before you pair: does adding one change it?
steps: Start with 6 counters (even). Before touching them, predict whether adding ONE more will keep it even or make it odd — and say why.
Add the counter and pair them up to check your prediction.
Explain the result using pairing: the new counter either finds a partner or is left alone.
activities.insight: Adding one counter to an even number leaves one unpaired, making it odd; the reason stated before checking shows whether a learner understands pairing or is only reading off a label afterwards.

checkQuestion: Here are 7 counters. Is 7 odd or even? Now here are 8 counters — is 8 odd or even? For each one, show me with the counters how you can tell.
checkAnswer: 7 is odd, 8 is even. A child reasoning correctly pairs the counters up (or splits into two equal groups): 8 makes 4 pairs with none left over, so it is even; 7 makes 3 pairs with one left over, so it is odd — even means it can be shared into two equal groups (or all paired) with nothing left, odd leaves one.
